steps.title: The goed-est day ever
paragraphs: Little Theo told his grandma about his day: “I goed to the zoo and I seed a lion! It eated a whole chicken. Then I runned to the monkeys.”
Theo is three, and he’s actually being very clever: he knows the past tense adds -ed, so he adds it to everything.
The trouble is that many of the most common English verbs are irregular. They don’t add -ed. They change: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, run → ran.

cards.title: Three forms to know
cards.body: Every verb has a base (go), a past (went) and a past participle (gone). Use the past on its own: “I went.” Use the participle after has/have/had: “I have gone.” For regular verbs, the past and participle are the same (walked, have walked). Irregular verbs can have three different forms.

cards.title: Irregular families
cards.text:
Vowel change (i → a → u): sing sang sung · swim swam swum · drink drank drunk · begin began begun
-ought/-aught: bring brought · think thought · buy bought · catch caught · teach taught
-en participle: eat ate eaten · write wrote written · take took taken · break broke broken
All the same: cut cut cut · put put put · hurt hurt hurt
cards.note: Learning them in families is easier than one by one.

cards.title: Past or participle?
cards.telling: I seen it. She done her best. We have went there. He had ran away.
cards.showing: I saw it. She did her best. We have gone there. He had run away.
cards.note: Seen, done, gone, been and taken never stand alone: they need has/have/had. And “should of” is always “should have”.

cards.title: Spot the made-up verbs
cards.prompt: Tap the three verbs that aren’t real words.
cards.text: We brang our lunches, but the seagulls stealed half of them. Then Dad buyed us pizza instead.

prompts: Which irregular verb family will you remember best? Give one example.
Which irregular verb do you most often get wrong, and how will you remember it?
